Week 17

Kicking & Striking: Power From the Ground Up 🦶

Kicking and striking are manipulative skills that use your legs and arms to hit an object. They share something in common with throwing: the power comes from a chain — but for kicks, the chain starts at your planted foot, not your throwing hand. For racket sports, your feet still set the foundation. The lesson is the same: get your base right, and the rest works.

1
Lesson 1
The Kicking Motion

A good kick uses your whole leg — and a little bit of your whole body. Here's the breakdown:

  1. Plant your non-kicking foot next to (not behind) the ball — about 6 inches to the side
  2. Lock your ankle on the kicking foot, toes pointed down
  3. Swing your kicking leg back — hip extends, knee bends
  4. Drive the leg forward — hip leads, knee follows, foot whips through last
  5. Strike with the laces (for power) or inside of foot (for accuracy)
  6. Follow through — kicking leg keeps going up after contact
🧪Sport Science

Cristiano Ronaldo's free kicks fly at over 70 mph because his kicking leg moves at about 20 meters per second at the moment of contact. That speed doesn't come from leg strength alone — it comes from a perfectly timed hip rotation, called the hip-to-knee separation. His hips start rotating before his knee straightens, which whips the foot through at maximum speed. Same physics as a baseball pitch or a tennis serve.

2
Lesson 2
Striking with the Hands or a Tool

Striking is hitting an object with your hand, a paddle, a bat, or a racket. It shows up in volleyball, tennis, baseball, hockey, pickleball, and more. The setup looks different depending on the sport, but the same body chain is at work:

  • Feet positioned for balance and power transfer
  • Hips rotate through the swing
  • Eyes on the contact point — never look up early
  • Follow through for power and accuracy
3
Lesson 3
Forehand, Backhand, Volley
➡️
Forehand
Strike on your dominant-hand side. Used for power shots in tennis, pickleball, table tennis.
⬅️
Backhand
Strike on your non-dominant side. Trickier — but essential for full-court coverage.
🏐
Volley
Strike the ball BEFORE it bounces. Quick reflexes, short stroke.
💡Did You Know?

A Major League Baseball player has roughly 0.4 seconds to decide whether to swing at a 95 mph fastball, where to swing, and to actually swing — all before the ball arrives. That's less time than it takes to blink. Hitting is one of the hardest skills in any sport, which is why even pros are considered great if they get a hit just 3 out of 10 times at bat.

4
Try It
Kick & Strike Drills
⚽
Wall Pass
Kick a ball at a wall and trap the return. 20 reps each foot.
🎯
Cone Targets
Set up 3 cones 10 feet away. Try to hit each by kicking accurately.
🏓
Paddle Bounce
Bounce a ball on a paddle 20 times without dropping it.
🏐
Wall Volley
Use your hand or paddle to keep a ball going against a wall, 10 in a row.
🌎Real-World Connection

Soccer goalkeepers can kick a ball over 200 feet downfield. Tennis pros serve at over 140 mph. The world record for the fastest hockey slap shot is over 100 mph. None of those came from raw strength — they came from years of practicing the same body chain you're starting now. The pros built on the basics. You're building the basics.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Striking — Hitting an object with your hand, a bat, or a racket.
  • Forehand — Striking on your dominant-hand side.
  • Backhand — Striking on your non-dominant side.
  • Volley — Striking a ball before it bounces.
  • Hip-to-knee separation — The hip starts rotating before the knee straightens — generates power (stretch term).
  • Follow-through — The motion after contact — adds power and accuracy.
📝Weekly Reflection

Why does the position of your non-kicking foot matter so much? Try kicking a ball with your plant foot in three different positions: behind the ball, beside it, ahead of it. How does each change the kick? What evidence does this give you about how your body uses leverage?

→What's Next

Next: design your own kicking or striking game in Week 18, then test your aim in Flight Club.

Unit 1.10

Teamwork & Cooperation: Multiply Your Strength 🤝

Most sports — and most jobs — are played in teams. A great individual on a team that doesn't cooperate usually loses to an average team that works together. Teamwork is a skill, just like throwing or sprinting. The good news? You can train it.

1
Lesson 1
What Cooperation Actually Looks Like

Cooperation isn't just "being nice." It's a set of specific behaviors that help a group reach a goal it couldn't reach alone:

  • Communication — saying what you'll do and listening to what others say
  • Role clarity — knowing what your job is and trusting others to do theirs
  • Shared goal — pushing toward the same outcome, even if individual stats don't shine
  • Adaptation — adjusting your plan when the situation changes

You see this in every relay race, soccer match, group project, and band rehearsal. The teams that move smoothly aren't accidentally smooth — they practice these specific skills.

2
Lesson 2
Roles on a Team

Healthy teams need a mix of roles. Some you'll be more naturally drawn to than others, but in 5th grade you should try them all:

🧭
Leader
Sets direction, makes the call when there's no time to discuss.
👂
Listener
Gathers ideas from quieter teammates, builds the plan.
🛠️
Builder
Takes the plan and executes — does the actual work.
🎤
Cheerleader
Keeps energy high, picks up teammates after mistakes.
🧰
Problem-Solver
Spots when the plan isn't working and suggests a fix.
🧪Sport Science

Researchers at Google studied hundreds of teams to find what made the best ones succeed. The number one factor wasn't talent. It wasn't experience. It was psychological safety — meaning every team member felt safe speaking up, admitting mistakes, and trying ideas. The same thing applies to PE: a team that lets its quietest player call a play is usually better than one that just listens to the loudest.

3
Lesson 3
What Breaks Teams

Knowing what doesn't work is just as important. Common team-breakers:

  • One person dominates and doesn't pass
  • Blaming teammates for mistakes
  • Not communicating — running silent
  • Refusing to play a role you don't love (every position matters)
  • Quitting after a setback

If you've seen these behaviors, you know how quickly they wreck a group. The good news: when you NOTICE them, you can choose differently.

💡Did You Know?

The U.S. Navy SEALs say their training is more about teamwork than individual skill. Recruits who are the strongest swimmers, fastest runners, or best shooters often fail SEAL training because they can't work with their team. The SEALs say a fast person who runs alone slows the whole team. A medium-speed person who keeps the team moving wins.

4
Try It
Cooperation Mini-Challenges
🪢
Human Knot
Group holds hands across a circle; untangle without letting go.
🎈
Balloon Keep-Up
Keep a balloon off the floor — but each person can only tap it once before someone else does.
📦
Group Carry
Move an object from A to B using only feet, or only one hand each.
🤐
Silent Build
Build a tower of cups as a team — but no one can talk.
🌎Real-World Connection

Surgical teams, fire crews, airline cockpit teams, and SWAT teams all run team training drills regularly — not because they're new, but because cooperation is a perishable skill. If they don't practice, they get rusty. Same with you: every game is a chance to practice, even if you've been on teams for years.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Teamwork — Working with others toward a shared goal.
  • Cooperation — Adjusting your actions to fit with what teammates are doing.
  • Communication — Clearly sharing information so the team can act together.
  • Role — Your specific job or position on a team.
  • Psychological safety — When everyone on a team feels safe speaking up (stretch term).
  • Adaptation — Adjusting your plan based on what's actually happening.
📝Weekly Reflection

Think of the BEST team experience you've had — and the worst. What was the team doing differently in each case? Pick the single behavior that made the biggest difference. How do you know it was that one? Use specific evidence from the game or activity.

→What's Next

Next: show your teamwork in action, then take on the Flight Club Leadership Challenge.

Unit 1.11

Sportsmanship & Respect: How Real Athletes Compete 🤝

Winning matters. But how you compete matters more — for one big reason: the way you act when you win and lose shapes how other people see you, and how you see yourself. Sportsmanship isn't a soft skill. It's the part of competition that builds your reputation and your character.

1
Lesson 1
What Sportsmanship Looks Like

Good sportsmanship has clear, observable behaviors:

  • Respect opponents — they're not enemies, they're the reason the game exists
  • Respect officials — referees miss calls; arguing rarely helps
  • Play by the rules — even when no one's watching
  • Win humbly — celebrate the win, not the loss of your opponent
  • Lose with dignity — congratulate the winner, learn from the loss

This isn't just etiquette. Sportsmanship is what keeps competition fun for everyone, season after season.

2
Lesson 2
Why Sportsmanship is Hard

Being a good sport is harder than it sounds because emotions run high in competition. When you lose, your brain releases stress chemicals. When you win, you feel a rush of dopamine. Both can make you act in ways you'd regret later — taunting an opponent, blaming a teammate, slamming equipment.

Athletes train themselves to NOTICE these urges and choose differently. That mental skill is called emotional regulation — controlling how you respond to strong feelings.

🧪Sport Science

When you lose a close game, the same brain regions activate as when you experience physical pain. That's why a tough loss can feel almost like getting hurt. Scientists who study athletes say the ability to stay composed after a loss — to "lose the right way" — is one of the strongest predictors of long-term success. The athletes who can regulate their emotions improve faster than those who can't.

3
Lesson 3
Respect Is Bigger Than Sports

The respect you practice in PE is the same respect you owe people everywhere — classmates, family, teachers, future coworkers. Specific behaviors:

  • Listen when others talk — don't cut them off
  • Use names — it shows you see the person
  • Acknowledge differences — different skills, backgrounds, viewpoints make teams stronger
  • Stand up for teammates — especially the ones who can't always speak up for themselves
💡Did You Know?

The Olympic Games include a specific award called the Pierre de Coubertin Medal, named after the founder of the modern Olympics. It's given to athletes who show outstanding sportsmanship — sometimes even when they LOSE the actual competition. Past winners have stopped during a race to help an opponent up. The Olympics value this so highly that the medal is considered as prestigious as gold.

4
Try It
Sportsmanship Self-Check

After your next game or PE activity, ask yourself:

  1. Did I congratulate at least one opponent or teammate?
  2. Did I follow the rules even when no one was looking?
  3. How did I act after a mistake — mine or someone else's?
  4. Would my teammates say I lifted them up or brought them down?
  5. If I lost, did I learn something I can use next time?
🌎Real-World Connection

Many sports — including the NFL and NBA — fine players for unsportsmanlike conduct. A single bad gesture or taunt can cost a player tens of thousands of dollars. Leagues do this because they know sportsmanship affects how the public sees the sport. The big leagues take sportsmanship as seriously as scoring.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Sportsmanship — Behaving with fairness, respect, and good grace in competition.
  • Respect — Treating others with consideration, even when you disagree or compete.
  • Integrity — Doing the right thing even when no one is watching.
  • Humility — Winning or succeeding without putting others down.
  • Emotional regulation — Managing how you react to strong feelings (stretch term).
  • Fair play — Following both the written and unwritten rules of a game.
📝Weekly Reflection

Describe a time you saw GREAT sportsmanship — and a time you saw the opposite. Why does it matter? How did each situation affect the other people involved? If you could go back to the bad moment, what would you have done differently — and how do you know it would have been better?

→What's Next

Next: write your sportsmanship reflection, then take the Flight Club Dice Challenge.

The 5 Fitness Components: The Athlete's Toolkit 🛠️

"Being in shape" means different things in different sports. A gymnast and a long-distance runner are both fit — but their fitness looks different. Sport scientists have broken fitness into five components. Most sports need all five, but each sport leans on certain ones more than others. Knowing your toolkit helps you train smart.

1
Lesson 1
The Five Components
🫀
Cardiovascular Endurance
How long your heart and lungs can fuel activity. Tested by running a mile.
💪
Muscular Strength
How much force your muscles can produce. Tested by push-ups, squats, or a max lift.
🔋
Muscular Endurance
How long your muscles can keep producing force. Tested by holding a plank or repeating sit-ups.
🤸
Flexibility
How far your joints can move. Tested by the sit-and-reach.
⚖️
Body Composition
The ratio of muscle, bone, water, and fat in your body. Hardest to measure, easiest to improve through movement + nutrition.
🧪Sport Science

The five components aren't independent — they affect each other. For example, you can't run a long distance (cardiovascular endurance) without leg muscles that don't fatigue (muscular endurance). Many coaches add skill-related components too: speed, power, balance, coordination, agility, and reaction time. Those are the bridge between fitness and actual sport performance.

2
Lesson 2
Which Sports Train Which Components
Sport Top Components
SoccerCardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, speed
GymnasticsFlexibility, muscular strength, balance
Football (offensive line)Muscular strength, power
Cross-country runningCardiovascular endurance
BasketballAll five, but especially cardio endurance + power
YogaFlexibility, muscular endurance, balance
3
Lesson 3
Your Personal Fitness Snapshot

You can test your own fitness components with simple at-home tests:

  • Cardiovascular endurance — time yourself running a mile
  • Muscular strength — how many push-ups in a row?
  • Muscular endurance — how long can you hold a plank?
  • Flexibility — sit-and-reach: can you touch your toes?
  • Body composition — track changes over time, not single measurements

Don't compare yourself to anyone else. The point is to see your baseline — and then watch it improve over a season.

💡Did You Know?

Decathletes — track and field athletes who compete in 10 events — are sometimes called "the most all-around fit humans on the planet" because they have to excel in events that demand opposite components (a strength event like shot put AND a long endurance event like the 1500m). Decathletes train all five components year-round, which is why their fitness is so well-rounded.

4
Lesson 4
Training the Components Together

The best workouts hit multiple components at once. Examples:

  • Obstacle course — strength (climbing) + endurance (running) + flexibility (crawling)
  • Circuit training — alternates strength moves with cardio bursts
  • Sport scrimmage — natural mix of cardio, strength, and skill
  • Yoga flow — flexibility + muscular endurance + balance
🌎Real-World Connection

Sports physical therapists assess all five fitness components when athletes recover from injury. A torn ACL might recover its strength quickly but lose flexibility — so the PT plans rehab to bring everything back into balance. The goal isn't one big number; it's a balanced toolkit. That's true for you too: don't just train your favorite component. Train the weakest one too.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Fitness component — One of the five categories that make up total fitness.
  • Cardiovascular endurance — How long your heart and lungs can sustain activity.
  • Muscular strength — Maximum force your muscles can produce in one effort.
  • Muscular endurance — How long your muscles can keep producing force.
  • Body composition — The ratio of muscle, fat, water, and bone in your body.
  • Power — How fast you can produce strength (a skill-related component, stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Sara plays soccer for 30 minutes, three times a week. She also does push-ups every morning. Which TWO fitness components is she training the most? How do you know? Now: which two are you training the most this month? Which component would you most like to improve, and why?

→What's Next

Next: complete the Fitness Component Station and design your fitness poster, then test your core in the Plank & Balance Flight Club.

Unit 1.13

Personal Space & Movement Safety: Play Smart, Stay Healthy 🛡️

The fastest athletes in the world have one thing in common: they don't get hurt often. Safety isn't a brake on performance — it's a foundation for it. Knowing how to read personal space, control your body, and avoid risks lets you push harder when it counts.

1
Lesson 1
What Personal Space Really Means

Personal space is the invisible bubble around your body that you control. In PE, it has two layers:

  • Physical bubble — about an arm's length around you when moving. Anything inside that bubble is at risk of a collision.
  • Social bubble — the comfortable distance for talking, listening, or working close. About 1.5–4 feet for most people.

In a fast game, your physical bubble shrinks because you're moving toward and around teammates and opponents. The skill is being aware of your bubble AND everyone else's at the same time.

2
Lesson 2
Spatial Awareness on the Field

Spatial awareness is your brain's ability to track where things are around you — not just in front. Strong spatial awareness lets you avoid collisions, find open passing lanes, and stay safe in chaotic moments.

To build it:

  • Scan the field — look around every few seconds, not just at the ball
  • Listen — sounds (footsteps, calls) give you info your eyes miss
  • Watch peripheral motion — your eyes can detect movement to the side without turning your head
  • Anticipate — predict where teammates and opponents will be in 2 seconds
🧪Sport Science

Hockey legend Wayne Gretzky was famous for being "where the puck was going to be, not where it was." Coaches called it a sixth sense, but really it was elite spatial awareness combined with pattern recognition — his brain had seen so many game situations that it could predict what came next. Your brain is wired to do this too, with practice. Every scrimmage, every game, builds the pattern library you draw from.

3
Lesson 3
Common Injuries — and How to Avoid Them
🦴
Sprains
Stretched or torn ligaments (often ankles). Avoid: warm up, watch your footing.
💢
Strains
Pulled muscles or tendons (often hamstrings). Avoid: warm up, build strength gradually.
💥
Collisions
Two players running into each other. Avoid: spatial awareness, communicate.
🧠
Concussions
A blow to the head that affects brain function. Tell a coach IMMEDIATELY if you feel dizzy or confused after impact.
💡Did You Know?

Sports doctors estimate that up to half of youth sports injuries are preventable with proper warm-up, technique, and rest. The number one cause of preventable injury? Doing too much, too fast. Athletes who add training intensity gradually — by no more than 10% per week — get hurt much less often than those who jump in at full speed.

4
Lesson 4
Safety Rules in PE

Every PE class has rules — they aren't there to slow you down, they're there to keep you in the game:

  1. Listen for instructions before starting
  2. Wear safe shoes — closed-toe, laced, with grip
  3. Stay in the assigned space — out-of-bounds is dangerous, not just illegal
  4. Use equipment correctly — bats are for hitting balls, not waving around
  5. Tell an adult if you see a hazard — wet floor, broken equipment, an injured player
  6. Hydrate — water before, during, and after
🌎Real-World Connection

Athletic trainers (ATCs) are the safety experts at high schools, colleges, and pro teams. Their job: assess injuries on the sideline, decide who plays and who sits, and design return-to-play plans. They're licensed medical professionals — and the rules they enforce in pro sports are based on the same principles you're learning now: warm up, hydrate, communicate, and respect the space around you.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Personal space — The area immediately around your body — your physical bubble.
  • Spatial awareness — Your brain's tracking of where things are around you (stretch term).
  • Sprain — A stretched or torn ligament — often at the ankle or wrist.
  • Strain — A pulled or torn muscle — often in the hamstring or calf.
  • Collision — When two objects (or players) come into contact unintentionally.
  • Hydration — Keeping enough water in your body for it to function well.
📝Weekly Reflection

What is the most common way kids get hurt in PE or sports you play? Why does it happen — is it about awareness, warm-up, equipment, or attitude? How could the player AND the coach have prevented it? Give specific evidence from a real situation you've seen or experienced.

→What's Next

Next: complete the VR Personal Space & Safety Signs activity and reflect on why it matters, then take the Jumping Jack Flight Club Countdown.

Unit 1.13

Water Safety & Basic Water Rescue 🌊

Swimming and paddling are some of the best ways to stay active for life — but water demands respect. Drowning is usually fast and silent, not the loud splashing you see in movies, and it can happen to strong swimmers too. Knowing how to help someone without putting yourself in danger is a skill every athlete in training should carry for life.

1
Lesson 1
Why Water Deserves Respect

Water is unforgiving in two ways most people underestimate. First, a person in trouble often can't call out — their energy goes into trying to breathe, so a real emergency is quiet. Second, cold water steals strength and breath control in seconds. That's why rules matter more around water than almost anywhere else in PE.

The goal of this lesson isn't to scare you — it's to make you the calm, useful person in an emergency instead of a second victim.

2
Lesson 2
The Golden Rule: Reach or Throw, Don't Go

If you see someone struggling, your instinct is to jump in. Don't. A panicking swimmer is surprisingly strong and may pull a rescuer underwater — that is how one emergency becomes two. The most important rule of water rescue is the same for kids and most adults: reach or throw, but don't go.

Your very first move is always to call for help — shout for a lifeguard or adult and call 911. You are most useful as the person who gets trained help fast.

🧪Sport Science

When a person can't keep their head above water, the body triggers a panic response: heart rate spikes, muscles clench, and they grab anything within reach with startling force. Cold water makes it worse — a sudden plunge causes an involuntary gasp and makes breath control hard even for strong swimmers. Reaching and throwing assists work because they let you help from a stable position the panic response can't drag you out of.

3
Lesson 3
Reaching and Throwing Assists

There are two safe ways to help from land, depending on how far away the person is:

🤚
Reaching assist
For someone close. Brace yourself on the deck or shore and extend a pole, paddle, branch, towel, pool noodle, or even your arm. Stay anchored so you can't be pulled in.
🎯
Throwing assist
For someone too far to reach. Throw something that floats — a life ring, life jacket, rope, ball, cooler, or empty jug — and aim just past them so it lands within reach.

Almost anything buoyant can become a rescue tool. The point is to give the person something to hold so they can keep their head up until trained help arrives.

💡Did You Know?

A flotation device is anything that floats well enough to keep a person's head above water. Lifeguards are trained to hand a struggling swimmer something to hold rather than grab them directly — the same "give them something to hold" logic you can use safely from shore.

4
Lesson 4
Prevent the Emergency in the First Place

The best rescue is the one you never have to make:

  • Always swim with a buddy and where a lifeguard can see you — the buddy system means someone always knows where you are.
  • Wear a properly fitted life jacket on boats and around open water.
  • Know your limits and stay in water you can handle.
  • Never play breath-holding games — they can cause swimmers to black out underwater.
  • Walk, don't run, on wet pool decks.
🌎Real-World Connection

Lifeguards train for months before they ever sit in the chair, and the first thing they learn is exactly what you just read: assess, call for help, then reach or throw before ever entering the water. The professionals follow the same rule you do — because it's the rule that keeps rescuers alive.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Water rescue — Helping someone out of the water using the safest method available.
  • Reaching assist — Extending an object to a person while you stay anchored on land.
  • Throwing assist — Tossing a floating object or line to a person too far to reach.
  • Flotation device — Anything buoyant that helps keep a person's head above water (stretch term).
  • Buddy system — Always swimming with a partner so someone knows where you are.
  • Lifeguard — A trained professional who prevents and responds to water emergencies.
📝Weekly Reflection

Why is "don't go" the rule even for strong swimmers? Use what you read about the panic response as your evidence. Then compare a reaching assist and a throwing assist — in what situation would each be the better choice, and why? Finally, name two objects in your own home you could use as a throwing assist, and explain what makes each one work.

→What's Next

Next: add water safety to your personal-safety toolkit alongside spatial awareness and PE safety rules. Smart athletes plan for the worst so they can enjoy the water without fear.

Unit 1.13

Cycling Safety: Visible, Predictable & Communicate 🚴

A bike is one of the few pieces of fitness equipment that's also transportation — it builds cardiovascular endurance and gets you where you're going. But the moment you ride near cars, you're sharing the road with vehicles that weigh thousands of pounds and can't stop instantly. Smart cyclists rely on three habits, not luck: be visible, be predictable, and communicate.

1
Lesson 1
Be Visible

A driver can only react to what they actually see. Being visible means being easy to spot, in daylight and especially at dusk or dark:

  • Wear bright colors during the day and reflective material at night.
  • Use a steady or flashing white light on the front and a red light on the back.
  • Add reflectors to your wheels, pedals, and frame.
  • Try to make eye contact at intersections — if you can't see the driver's eyes, assume they can't see you.
2
Lesson 2
Be Predictable

Being predictable means moving the way drivers expect, so they can plan around you:

  • Ride in a straight line — don't weave between parked cars.
  • Ride with traffic, in the same direction as cars, never against it.
  • Obey the same signs and signals that cars do, including stop signs and red lights.
  • Slow down and check before you change position on the road.
💡Did You Know?

The three habits work as a system. Being visible gets you noticed, being predictable lets drivers anticipate your next move, and communicating confirms it. Drop any one and a driver is left reacting to a surprise — which is exactly when crashes happen.

3
Lesson 3
Communicate With Hand Signals

Cars have blinkers and brake lights; on a bike, you are the signal. Tell people what you're about to do before you do it:

⬅️
Left turn
Left arm straight out to the side.
➡️
Right turn
Right arm straight out (or left arm bent upward at the elbow).
🛑
Stopping
Left arm bent downward, palm facing back.

Look back, make eye contact, and signal early enough that a driver has time to react.

4
Lesson 4
Protect the Athlete's Most Important Equipment

Your brain runs every skill you've trained this year, and it doesn't heal like a scraped knee. A helmet isn't optional gear — fit it correctly every ride:

  • Two fingers of space between your eyebrows and the helmet's front edge.
  • Side straps form a "V" just under each ear.
  • The buckled chin strap leaves room for about two fingers under your chin.
  • The helmet sits level and doesn't slide when you shake your head.
🧪Sport Science

In a crash, your head stops suddenly but your brain keeps moving for an instant inside your skull. A helmet's foam layer crushes on impact, stretching that sudden stop over a few extra milliseconds and absorbing energy that would otherwise reach your brain. That tiny bit of extra stopping time is why a correctly fitted helmet dramatically lowers the risk of serious head injury.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Visible — Easy for drivers and others to see, day or night.
  • Predictable — Moving the way others expect, so they can plan around you.
  • Hand signal — Using your arm to communicate a turn or stop before you make it.
  • Reflector — A surface that bounces light back toward its source so you show up in headlights.
  • Right-of-way — The rules that decide who goes first at intersections and crossings.
📝Weekly Reflection

Why does riding with traffic and in a straight line make you safer? Explain the logic a driver goes through when a cyclist is predictable. pages.html:

Unit 1.14

Rhythmic Movement & Dance: Move to the Beat 🎵

Dance and rhythmic movement aren't just for performance — they're some of the best full-body training out there. They develop coordination, timing, and body awareness in ways no other type of training can match. Professional athletes from Steph Curry to Serena Williams have used dance to sharpen their footwork.

1
Lesson 1
What Rhythmic Movement Means

Rhythmic movement is moving your body to a steady beat or pattern. It can be as simple as clapping along to a song or as complex as a dance routine. Either way, your brain has to:

  • Hear (or feel) the beat
  • Predict when the next beat is coming
  • Tell your muscles to move on that beat — not before or after

That timing skill is harder than it looks, which is why so many athletes train it on purpose.

2
Lesson 2
Why Dance Helps Athletes

Dance training improves several skills that show up in nearly every sport:

🦶
Footwork
Quick, precise foot positions — the foundation of boxing, tennis, basketball defense.
⚖️
Balance
Holding positions on one foot, switching weight smoothly.
⏱️
Timing
Coordinating movement with external signals (the beat, an opponent, a ball).
🧠
Memory
Remembering and chaining sequences — useful for plays and routines.
💃
Body control
Knowing exactly where every limb is at any moment.
🧪Sport Science

NFL wide receivers often take ballet classes during the off-season — yes, ballet. Why? Because ballet is the ultimate training for footwork, balance, and body control. Players who add dance to their training have measurably better agility scores. The same is true for boxers, who use jump rope and footwork drills built around music. The beat trains the body to move with timing under pressure.

3
Lesson 3
Tempo, Beat, and Pattern

Music has structure you can use to move:

  • Beat — the steady "pulse" you naturally tap to
  • Tempo — how fast the beat goes (slow songs vs. fast songs)
  • Pattern — how beats group together (most music groups in sets of 4)

If you can hear those three things, you can dance. The rest is just style.

💡Did You Know?

Humans are the only species besides parrots and a few other birds that can "keep a beat" — moving in sync with an external rhythm. Scientists call this beat-induction ability. Other primates, including chimpanzees, generally can't do it. It's connected to language and complex social behavior. So when you dance with friends, you're using one of the most uniquely human skills in nature.

4
Lesson 4
Try It — Simple Rhythm Drills
👏
Clap Pattern
Play a song. Clap on every beat for 30 seconds. Then clap only on beats 1 and 3.
🏀
Dribble to a Beat
Bounce a ball on each beat of a song. Try faster songs.
🦶
Footwork Box
Step front, side, back, side — on each beat. Easy at slow tempo, hard at fast.
🕺
Mirror Move
With a partner, take turns copying each other's moves to the beat.
🌎Real-World Connection

Cheer squads, marching bands, drill teams, and color guards all combine athleticism with rhythmic movement. Many also compete at high levels — cheer is one of the most physically demanding sports there is, with all the strength, flexibility, and timing of gymnastics combined with team coordination. If you've ever thought "dance isn't a sport," watch a competitive cheer routine.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Rhythmic movement — Moving your body to a steady beat or pattern.
  • Beat — The steady pulse that drives the rhythm.
  • Tempo — How fast the beat goes.
  • Coordination — The smooth working-together of body parts during movement.
  • Timing — Acting at the right moment — neither too early nor too late.
  • Body awareness — Your sense of how your body is positioned and moving (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Are you more comfortable moving FAST or SLOW to a beat? Why? Pick a song you know. Try dancing to a section at normal speed, then at half speed, then at double speed. Which felt easier? How do you know — what specific moves got harder or simpler?

→What's Next

Next: reflect on your dance experience and put rhythm in motion, then take the Flight Club Wall Sit Countdown.

pages.html:

Unit 1.15

Balance & Coordination: The Invisible Skills ⚖️

Balance and coordination are the quiet skills behind every athletic move. You don't see them on a scoreboard — but the moment they fail, you trip, drop, or get blocked. Athletes who look "smooth" almost always have well-trained balance and coordination. The best news? Both can be trained at home with no equipment.

1
Lesson 1
Static vs. Dynamic Balance

Sport scientists describe two kinds of balance:

  • Static balance — holding a position without moving. Example: standing on one foot.
  • Dynamic balance — keeping balance while moving. Example: running on a balance beam, skateboarding, dribbling a soccer ball.

Sports almost always need dynamic balance — but static balance is the foundation. If you can't hold a still position, you can't control a moving one.

🧪Sport Science

Your sense of balance comes from three sources working together: your eyes (visual feedback), your inner ear (which has fluid-filled tubes that detect head motion), and your proprioception (sensors in your joints and muscles that report position). When one source fails — like closing your eyes — the other two have to work harder. That's why balancing on one foot is so much harder with your eyes shut.

2
Lesson 2
What Coordination Means

Coordination is the smooth working-together of body parts during movement. There are several specific types:

👁️
Hand-Eye
Tracking with your eyes while your hands do something — catching, throwing, hitting.
👣
Foot-Eye
Same idea, but with feet — soccer dribbling, jumping over obstacles.
👐
Bilateral
Both sides of your body working together — swimming, jumping rope, rowing.
🔄
Cross-Lateral
Opposite arm and leg coordinating — walking, running, swimming a freestyle stroke.
3
Lesson 3
Why Athletes Train These on Purpose

If a goalkeeper has bad hand-eye, they don't catch shots. If a soccer player has bad foot-eye, they trip over the ball. If a swimmer has bad bilateral coordination, their stroke is uneven. Athletes train coordination because raw strength alone doesn't make a great move — strength combined with coordination does.

💡Did You Know?

Babies don't have coordination at birth — they develop it month by month. First they figure out how to track an object with their eyes (about 3 months). Then how to reach for it (about 5 months). Then how to bring their hands together (about 6 months). By age 1, they can pick something up. The same building-block process happens with new sports skills, just much faster — practice builds the pathways your brain needs.

4
Try It
Balance & Coordination Drills
🦩
One-Foot Stand
Hold for 30 sec, then try with eyes closed. Switch feet.
🚶
Heel-to-Toe Walk
Walk a straight line, heel touching toe. 20 steps.
🦵
Stork Stand
Stand on one foot, other foot on your knee. Hold 30 sec each side.
🤹
Ball Toss
Toss a ball up, catch with both hands. Then ONE hand. Then add a clap.
🦘
Hop-Stick
Hop forward on one foot — stick the landing without bobbing. Try eyes closed.
🌎Real-World Connection

Olympic figure skaters land jumps from heights of 2+ feet on a quarter-inch metal blade — and they have to stick the landing while spinning, all while looking smooth. That's dynamic balance, body awareness, and coordination working at the highest level humans have ever reached. They got there by training the same drills above, plus thousands of harder ones, for a decade.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Balance — The ability to control your body's position.
  • Static balance — Holding a still position without falling.
  • Dynamic balance — Keeping balance while moving (stretch term).
  • Coordination — Smooth, organized movement of multiple body parts.
  • Hand-eye coordination — Eyes and hands working together accurately.
  • Proprioception — Your body's internal sense of where its parts are (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Which is your weaker skill — balance or coordination? Try one drill from this lesson. Time yourself or count reps. Try the same drill in three days. Did you improve? Why or why not? What's your evidence that practice made a difference (or didn't)?

→What's Next

Next: experience and analyze your balance + coordination, then take the Wall Ball Toss Flight Club Challenge.

Unit 1.16

Goal Setting & Personal Fitness Plans: Train Like a Pro 🎯

Up to now, you've learned what fitness is. Now you'll learn how to plan your own training. Real athletes don't just "work out." They set specific goals, design plans, track progress, and adjust based on results. By the end of this unit, you'll have your own personal fitness plan — built by you, for you.

1
Lesson 1
Why Goal Setting Works

Goal setting isn't magic — it's psychology. When you set a clear, written goal, three things happen in your brain:

  • Your brain pays more attention to information related to the goal
  • You make better decisions when faced with choices ("Should I practice or watch TV?")
  • You can measure progress — which keeps you motivated

Studies show people who write down goals are 2–3 times more likely to achieve them than those who just think about them. Writing forces specificity. Specificity makes progress measurable.

2
Lesson 2
SMART Goals

The most-used framework for goal setting is SMART:

🎯
Specific
Clear and detailed. Not "get fit" but "do 20 push-ups in a row."
📏
Measurable
You can count or measure progress. Number of push-ups, time to run a mile.
✅
Achievable
Challenging but possible. Not "run a marathon next week" but "run a mile in 9 minutes by spring."
🎢
Relevant
Matters to YOU. Connected to a sport, hobby, or value.
⏰
Time-bound
Has a deadline. "By the end of the month" beats "someday."

Example of a SMART goal: "I will run a mile in under 9 minutes by April 30, by jogging 20 minutes three times a week."

🧪Sport Science

Olympic athletes work with sport psychologists who help them set process goals (things you control day-to-day, like "stretch 10 minutes daily") AND outcome goals (results, like "win the gold"). The trick: focus your daily attention on process goals. Outcomes follow process. If you focus only on the outcome, you skip the steps that actually create it.

3
Lesson 3
Building a Personal Fitness Plan

A personal fitness plan has five parts:

  1. Goal — written in SMART format
  2. Components to train — which of the 5 fitness components matter most for this goal?
  3. Weekly schedule — which days, which activities, how long?
  4. Progress checks — when and how will you measure progress?
  5. Adjustments — what will you change if you're not progressing?

Don't make a plan so packed you can't keep up. A plan you actually follow beats a perfect plan you abandon.

💡Did You Know?

NFL teams plan their seasons years in advance, using something called periodization — alternating phases of building strength, building speed, building endurance, and recovering. Pro athletes don't try to be at peak fitness all year; they peak for the games that matter. Your fitness plan should do the same: train hard, but build in rest days. Recovery is part of the plan, not the absence of one.

4
Lesson 4
Tracking and Adjusting

The fanciest goal in the world fails if you don't track progress. Athletes use:

  • A simple log — date, activity, duration, how it felt
  • Periodic tests — re-test the goal every 2 weeks
  • Feedback partners — a coach, friend, or family member who checks in

And don't be afraid to adjust. If progress is faster than expected, set a tougher goal. If progress is slower, change the plan, not the goal.

🌎Real-World Connection

The strongest athletes — and most successful adults — usually share one habit: regular self-review. Olympians keep journals. Surgeons review their cases. Software engineers do "code reviews." All of them ask the same questions you should ask: "What worked? What didn't? What will I do differently next time?" This is called metacognition — thinking about your own thinking. It's one of the most powerful tools in human learning.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Goal — An outcome you're working toward.
  • SMART — A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
  • Personal fitness plan — Your written plan for training toward a fitness goal.
  • Process goal — A goal about daily actions you control (stretch term).
  • Outcome goal — A goal about a result you want to achieve (stretch term).
  • Metacognition — Thinking about your own thinking — reviewing your own progress (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Write one SMART fitness goal for the next 30 days. Make sure it hits all five SMART criteria — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound. Now answer: how do you know your goal is achievable? What evidence do you have from your current fitness level? Why does this goal matter to YOU specifically?

→What's Next

Next: build your Personal Fitness Plan and create a fitness goal art project to lock it in.

  1. Get into a plank position: hands on the floor under your shoulders, body straight from your head to your toes, and tighten your tummy.
  2. Hold the plank for as long as you can while keeping good form.
    • Don't let your hips drop or lift too high.
    • Keep breathing!
  3. Stop when it gets too hard to keep your body straight.
  4. Try again later and see if you can hold it longer than before.
3
Try These Variations
  • Side Plank: Lie on your side and lift your body on one arm and the side of your foot. Switch sides after a few seconds.
  • Leg Lift Plank: Lift one leg while holding a plank. Switch legs every few seconds.
  • Partner Plank: Face a friend and try to hold your planks at the same time. Cheer each other on!
4
What You're Practicing
  • Muscles & Strength: Strong arms, shoulders, and core muscles
  • Endurance: Muscles that can work longer without getting tired
  • Balance & Control: Staying steady and moving safely

Tips:

  • Focus on quality over time — it's better to hold a good plank than a long, sloppy one.
  • Cheer your friends if you're in pairs or a group.
  • Beginners can try a knee plank or a forearm plank instead of the full plank.
✅Flight Crew Check-In

Flight Crew, check in!

  • This challenge trains TWO fitness components at once. Which two? How do you know?
  • Which version was hardest for you? Why — was it strength, endurance, or balance that gave out first?

🚀 Jumping Jack Flight Club Countdown

Cardio challenge with safety focus. Personal space matters here — make sure you have enough room to swing your arms and legs.

1
Your Goal

Get your heart and lungs working while having fun! Jumping jacks help improve cardiorespiratory endurance, which is your body's ability to keep moving without getting tired.

2
How to Play
  1. Stand with your feet together and your arms at your sides.
  2. Jump your feet out and raise your arms above your head at the same time.
  3. Jump back to your starting position. This is one jumping jack.
  4. Do as many jumping jacks as you can in 30–60 seconds while keeping good form.
    • Keep your core tight
    • Land softly on your feet
    • Breathe steadily
3
Variations & Challenges
  • Countdown Challenge: Start at 50 (or another number) and count down as you complete each jumping jack.
  • High Jumping Jacks: Jump a little higher or add a clap above your head for extra fun.
  • Slow & Steady: Go slower and focus on form and control.
  • Partner Challenge: Do jumping jacks side by side and cheer each other on.
4
Fitness Focus + Safety

Fitness Focus:

  • Cardiorespiratory Endurance: Strengthens your heart and lungs
  • Coordination: Helps your arms and legs move together
  • Energy & Stamina: Makes it easier to keep moving in games and activities

Tips:

  • Make sure there is enough space around you — personal space is important!
  • Keep your movements controlled and safe.
  • Take breaks if you get tired and try again.
🏃Activity Cue

Reflection Questions:

  • How many jumping jacks could you do in 30–60 seconds?
  • Did your heart beat faster or slower during the challenge?
  • How did keeping a steady pace help you do more?
  • Which variation did you like best and why?
✅Flight Crew Check-In

Flight Crew, check in!

Unit 1.14
🚀 Wall Sit Flight Club Countdown

Lower-body endurance test. Stand against a wall, slide down, and hold. It looks easy until the burn starts.

1
How to Play
  1. Find a clear wall space.
  2. Lean your back against the wall and slide down until your thighs are parallel to the floor, as if sitting in an invisible chair. Keep your knees directly above your ankles and your back flat against the wall.
  3. Hold this "chair" position for as long as you can, focusing on keeping good form.
2
Countdown Variation
  • Start by holding the position while counting down from a certain number (e.g., 30, 20, or 10 seconds).
  • Challenge yourself to reach zero without letting your thighs rise above parallel.
3
Difficulty Enhancements
  • Add a ball: Hold a small ball between your knees to engage inner thigh muscles.
  • Raise your hands: Extend your arms straight out in front of you or overhead to engage shoulders and core.
  • Single-leg lift: Carefully lift one foot off the ground for a few seconds, then switch legs to increase difficulty and balance challenge.
4
Safety Tips & Focus

Fitness Focus:

  • Muscular endurance: Keeps your thigh muscles working over time.
  • Strength: Strengthens quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and core.
  • Balance & focus: Helps improve stability and concentration while holding the position.

Safety Tips:

  • Avoid letting your knees go past your toes.
  • Keep your back flat against the wall.
  • Stop if you feel pain (muscle burn is okay, sharp pain is not).

Personal Challenge: Record how long you can hold the wall sit each day and try to improve your time. Think about which variations felt easiest or hardest and why.

✅Flight Crew Check-In

Flight Crew, check in!

  • Which muscle group did this challenge target the most — quads, hamstrings, or glutes? How do you know?
  • This is muscular endurance training, not strength. Why? Use what you've learned about reps, resistance, and time.

assignments.html:

Unit 1.15
🚀 Wall Ball Toss Flight Club Challenge

Balance + coordination + reaction time, all in one. The wall is your teammate. Don't break anything.

1
What You Need
  • A small, soft ball (foam ball, tennis ball, or rolled-up socks)
  • A clear wall space with nothing breakable nearby
2
How to Play
  1. Stand a few steps away from a wall.
  2. Toss the ball gently against the wall using both hands.
  3. Watch the ball carefully and catch it after it bounces back.
  4. Repeat for a set number of catches or for 30–60 seconds.

Focus on using soft hands when catching and keeping your eyes on the ball at all times.

3
Variations (Choose One or More)
  • One-Hand Catch: Toss with two hands and catch with only one hand. Switch hands after 10 catches.
  • Speed Toss: Toss and catch the ball faster while staying in control.
  • Squat & Catch: Perform one squat after each catch before tossing the ball again.
  • Clap & Catch: Toss the ball, clap once, then catch it.
  • Balance Toss: Stand on one foot while tossing and catching the ball. Switch feet halfway through.
4
Safety + Fitness Focus

Safety Tips:

  • Use a soft ball and throw gently (we're not trying to put a hole in the wall!).
  • Make sure the area around you is clear.
  • If the ball goes too far, slow down and regain control before continuing.

Fitness Focus:

  • Coordination: Helps hands and eyes work together.
  • Reaction Time: Improves quick responses to moving objects.
  • Upper Body Strength: Builds arm and shoulder muscles through repeated tossing and catching.

Challenge Option: See how many clean catches you can complete in 30 seconds. Try to beat your own score next time!

✅Flight Crew Check-In

Flight Crew, check in!

  • The Balance Toss variation tests two skills at once. Which two — and which one limited your reps first? How do you know?
  • How did your hand-eye coordination change over the challenge? Did you get smoother — what evidence do you have?

answers.text: A hop uses two feet to land; a leap uses one.

Plant his right foot BESIDE the ball (about 6 inches to the side), so his hips can rotate through the kick.
Wear different shoes — that's the only thing that affects soccer kicks.
Kick with both feet at the same time.
